trachearia: A division of Arachnida including those that breathe only by means of tracheæ. It includes the mites, ticks, false scorpions, and harvestmen.
transitorily: In a transitory manner; with brief continuance.
trade: 1. A track; a trail; a way; a path; also, passage; travel; resort. (old) A postern with a blind wicket there was, A common trade to pass through Priam's house. Surrey. | 1. To barter, or to buy and sell; to be engaged in the exchange, purchase, or sale of goods, wares, merchandise, or anything else; to traffic; to bargain; to carry on commerce as a business.
triobolary: Of the value of three oboli; hence, mean; worthless. (old) It may pass current . . . for a triobolar ballad. Cheyne.
triniunity: Triunity; trinity. (old) As for terms of trinity, triniunity, . . . and the like, they reject them as scholastic notions. Milton.
trioxide: An oxide containing three atoms of oxygen; as, sulphur trioxide, SO3; -- formerly called tritoxide.
trilling: 1. One of tree children born at the same birth. Wright. 2. (Crystallog.) A compound crystal, consisting of three individuals.
trist: 1. Trust. (old) 2. A post, or station, in hunting. (old) Chaucer. 3. A secret meeting, or the place of such meeting; a tryst. See Tryst. (old) George Douglas caused a trist to be set between him and… | Sad; sorrowful; gloomy. (old) Fairfax.
truculency: The quality or state of being truculent; savageness of manners; ferociousness.
trunksteamer: A freight steamer having a high hatch coaming extending almost continuously fore and aft, but not of whaleback form at the sides.
truttaceous: Of, pertaining to, or resembling, a trout; as, fish of the truttaceous kind.
treatise: 1. A written composition on a particular subject, in which its principles are discussed or explained; a tract. Chaucer. He published a treatise in which he maintained that a marriage between a member of the Church of England and a dissenter was a nullity. Macaulay.
triploidite: A manganese phosphate near triplite, but containing hydroxyl instead of fluorine.
trullization: The act of laying on coats of plaster with a trowel.
trough: 1. A long, hollow vessel, generally for holding water or other liquid, especially one formed by excavating a log longitudinally on one side; a long tray; also, a wooden channel for conveying water, as to a mill wheel. 2. Any channel, receptacle, or depression, of a long and narrow shape; as, trough between two ridges, etc.
troweled: Formed with a trowel; smoothed with a trowel; as, troweled stucco, that is, stucco laid on and ready for the reception of paint. [Written also trowelled.]
triplet: 1. A collection or combination of three of a kind; three united. 2. (Poetry) Three verses rhyming together. 3. (Mus.) A group of three notes sung or played in the tree of two. 4. pl. Three children or offspring born at one birth.
tricycle: A three-wheeled velocipede. See Illust. under Velocipede. Cf. Bicycle.
trueborn: Of genuine birth; having a right by birth to any title; as, a true-born Englishman.
transferability: The quality or state of being transferable.
tropology: A rhetorical mode of speech, including tropes, or changes from the original import of the word. Sir T. Browne.
trichophore: 1. (Bot.) The special cell in red algæ which produces or bears a trichogyne. See Illust. of Trichogyne. 2. (Zoöl.) One of the saclike organs from which the setæ of annelids arise. -- Trich`o*phor"ic, a.
tragus: The prominence in front of the external opening of the ear. See Illust. under Ear.
transfuse: 1. To pour, as liquid, out of one vessel into another; to transfer by pouring. 2 2 (Med.) To transfer, as blood, from the veins or arteries of one man or animal to those of another. 3. To cause to pass from to another; to cause to be instilled or imbibed; as, to transfuse a spirit of patriotism into a man; to transfuse a love of letters.
treasurer: One who has the care of a treasure or treasure or treasury; an officer who receives the public money arising from taxes and duties, or other sources of revenue, takes charge of the same, and disburses it upon orders made by the proper authority; one who has charge of collected funds; as, the treasurer of a society or corporation.
trais: Traces. (old) Four white bulls in the trays. Chaucer.
tragopan: Any one of several species of Asiatic pheasants of the genus Ceriornis. They are brilliantly colored with a variety of tints, the back and breast are usually covered with white or buff ocelli, and the head is ornamented with two bright-colored, fleshy wattles. The crimson tragopan, or horned pheasant (C. satyra), of India is one of the best-known species.
trover: (a) The gaining possession of any goods, whether by finding or by other means. (b) An action to recover damages against one who found goods, and would not deliver them to the owner on demand; an action which lies in any case to recover the value of goods wrongfully converted by another to his own use. In this case the finding, though alleged, is an immaterial fact;
trigeminous: Born three together; being one of three born at the same birth; also, threefold. E. Phillip
transplantation: 1. The act of transplanting, or the state of being transplanted; also, removal. The transplantation of Ulysses to Sparta. Broome. 2. (Surg.) The removal of tissues from a healthy part, and the insertion of them in another place where there is a lesion; as, the transplantation of tissues in autoplasty. 3.
tractorpropeller: A propeller screw placed in front of the supporting planes of an aëroplane instead of behind them, so that it exerts a pull instead of a push. Hence, Tractor monoplane, Tractor biplane, etc.
traditor: A deliverer; -- a name of infamy given to Christians who delivered the Scriptures, or the goods of the church, to their persecutors to save their lives. Milner.
trowelful: As much as a trowel will hold; enough to fill a trowel.
transmutation: 1. The act of transmuting, or the state of being transmuted; as, the transmutation of metals. 2. (Geom.) The change or reduction of one figure or body into another of the same area or solidity, but of a different form, as of a triangle into a square. 3. (Biol.) The change of one species into another, which is assumed to take place in any development theory of life;
tracer: One who, or that which, traces.
triptote: A noun having three cases only.
triliteral: Consisting of three letters; trigrammic; as, a triliteral root or word. -- n. A triliteral word.
tricliniary: Of or pertaining to a triclinium, or to the ancient mode of reclining at table.
tricrotism: That condition of the arterial pulse in which there is a triple beat. The pulse curve obtained in the sphygmographic tracing characteristic of tricrotism shows two secondary crests in addition to the primary.
tradesfolk: People employed in trade; tradesmen. Swift.
trisaccharide: A complex sugar, as raffinose, yielding by hydrolysis three simple sugar molecules.
tramontane: Lying or being beyond the mountains; coming from the other side of the mountains; hence, foreign; barbarous. Note: The Italians sometimes use this epithet for ultramontane, and apply it to the… | One living beyond the mountains; hence, a foreigner; a stranger.
trill: To flow in a small stream, or in drops rapidly succeeding each other; to trickle. Sir W. Scott. And now and then an ample tear trilled down Her delicate cheek. Shak. | To turn round; to twirl. (old) Gascoigne. Bid him descend and trill another pin. Chaucer.
trunk: 1. The stem, or body, of a tree, apart from its limbs and roots; the main stem, without the branches; stock; stalk. About the mossy trunk I wound me soon, For, high from ground, the branches would… | 1. To lop off; to curtail; to truncate; to maim. (old) "Out of the trunked stock." Spenser. 2. (Mining) To extract (ores) from the slimes in which they are contained, by means of a trunk.
trellis: A structure or frame of crossbarred work, or latticework, used for various purposes, as for screens or for supporting plants.
trinitarian: Of or pertaining to the Trinity, the doctrine of the Trinity, or believers in that doctrine. | 1. One who believes in the doctrine of the Trinity. 2. (Eccl. Hist.) One of a monastic order founded in Rome in 1198 by St. John of Matha, and an old French hermit, Felix of Valois, for the purpose…
trek: 1. To draw or haul a load, as oxen. 2. To travel, esp. by ox wagon; to go from place to place; to migrate. [Chiefly South Africa] One of the motives which induced the Boers of 1836 to trek out of the… | The act of trekking; a drawing or a traveling; a journey; a migration. [Chiefly South Africa] To the north a trek was projected, and some years later was nearly carried out, for the occupation of the…
truckle: A small wheel or caster. Hudibras. | To yield or bend obsequiously to the will of another; to submit; to creep. "Small, trucking states." Burke. Religion itself is forced to truckle to worldly poliey. Norris.
trichogyne: The slender, hairlike cell which receives the fertilizing particles, or antherozoids, in red seaweeds. -- Trich`o*gyn"ic, a.
trachytic: Of, pertaining to, or resembling, trachyte.
tribunary: Of or pertaining to tribunes; as, tribunary powers or authority.
trivium: 1. The three " liberal" arts, grammar, logic, and rhetoric; -- being a triple way, as it were, to eloquence. Note: The trivium and quadrivium together made up the seven liberal arts. See Quadrivium. 2. (Zoöl.) The three anterior ambulacra of echinoderms, collectively.
tradeful: Full of trade; busy in traffic; commercial. Spenser.
trucker: One who trucks; a trafficker. No man having ever yet driven a saving bargain with this great trucker for souls. South.
tremolite: A white variety of amphibole, or hornblende, occurring in long, bladelike crystals, and coarsely fibrous masses.
transpare: To be, or cause to be, transparent; to appear, or cause to appear, or be seen, through something. (old) Stirling.
trochil: The crocodile bird. The crocodile . . . opens his chaps to let the trochil in to pick his teeth, which gives it the usual feeding. Sir T. Herbert.
triplication: 1. The act of tripling, or making threefold, or adding three together. Glanvill. 2. (Civil Law) Same as Surrejoinder.
transmigration: 1. The act of passing from one country to another; migration. 2. The passing of the soul at death into another mortal body; metempsychosis.
treasonous: Treasonable. Shak. The treasonous book of the Court of King James. Pepys.
trepanner: One who trepans. " Pitiful trepanners and impostors." Gauden.
tropic: Of, pertaining to, or designating, an acid obtained from atropine and certain other alkaloids, as a white crystalline substance slightly soluble in water. | 1. (Astron.) One of the two small circles of the celestial sphere, situated on each side of the equator, at a distance of 23º 28min, and parallel to it, which the sun just reaches at its greatest…
trionyx: A genus of fresh-water or river turtles which have the shell imperfectly developed and covered with a soft leathery skin. They are noted for their agility and rapacity. Called also soft tortoise, soft-shell tortoise, and mud turtle. Note: The common American species (Trionyx, or Aspidonectus, ferox) becomes over a foot in length and is very voracious.
transvasation: The act or process of pouring out of one vessel into another. (old) Holland.
trouvere: One of a school of poets who flourished in Northern France from the eleventh to the fourteenth century.
triticum: A genus of grasses including the various species of wheat.
tripinnatifid: Thrice pinnately cleft; -- said of a pinnatifid leaf when its segments are pinnatifid, and the subdivisions of these also are pinnatifid.
trichomatose: Affected with a disease which causes agglutination and matting together; -- said of the hair when affected with plica. See Plica, 1.
trojan: Of or pertaining to ancient Troy or its inhabitants. -- n. A native or inhabitant of Troy. Tim jumped like a Trojan from the bed. Finnegan's Wake (Irish song)
trenchmore: A kind of lively dance of a rude, boisterous character. Also, music in triple time appropriate to the dance. (old) All the windows in the town dance new trenchmore. Beau. & Fl. | To dance the trenchmore. (old) Marston.
transfer: 1. To convey from one place or person another; to transport, remove, or cause to pass, to another place or person; as, to transfer the laws of one country to another; to transfer suspicion. 2. | 1. The act of transferring, or the state of being transferred; the removal or conveyance of a thing from one place or person to another. 2. (Law) The conveyance of right, title, or property, either…
truckage: The practice of bartering goods; exchange; barter; truck. The truckage of perishing coin. Milton. | Money paid for the conveyance of goods on a truck; freight.
tropism: Modification of the direction of growth.
trance: 1. A tedious journey. [Prov. Eng.] Halliwell. 2. A state in which the soul seems to have passed out of the body into another state of being, or to be rapt into visions; an ecstasy. | 1. To entrance. And three I left him tranced. Shak. 2. To pass over or across; to traverse. (poetic) Trance the world over. Beau. & Fl. When thickest dark did trance the sky. Tennyson.
triptych: Anything in three parts or leaves. Specifically: -- (a) A writing tablet in three parts, two of which fold over on the middle part. (b) A picture or altarpiece in three compartments.
trigerprocess: A method of sinking through water-bearing ground, in which the shaft is lined with tubbing and provided with an air lock, work being proceeded with under air pressure.
tracing: 1. The act of one who traces; especially, the act of copying by marking on thin paper, or other transparent substance, the lines of a pattern placed beneath; also, the copy thus producted. 2. A regular path or track; a course.
trimorph: A substance which crystallizes in three distinct forms, or which has three distinct physical states; also, any one of these distinct forms. See Trimorphism, 1.
transprose: To change from prose into verse; to versify; also, to change from verse into prose. (old) Dryden.
tribunitian: Of or pertaining to tribunes; befitting a tribune; as, tribunitial power or authority. Dryden. A kind of tribunician veto, forbidding that which is recognized to be wrong. Hare.
train: 1. To draw along; to trail; to drag. In hollow cube Training his devilish enginery. Milton. 2. To draw by persuasion, artifice, or the like; to attract by stratagem; to entice; to allure. | 1. To be drilled in military exercises; to do duty in a military company. 2. To prepare by exercise, diet, instruction, etc., for any physical contest; as, to train for a boat race.
trigonometrical: Of or pertaining to trigonometry; performed by the rules of trigonometry. --Trig`o*no*met"ric*al*ly, adv. Trigonometrical curve, a curve one of whose coördinates is a trigonometric function of the other. -- Trigonometrical function. See under Function.
tragedian: 1. A writer of tragedy. Thence what the lofty, grave, tragedians taught. Milton. 2. An actor or player in tragedy. Shak.
trisagion: An ancient anthem, -- usually known by its Latin name tersanctus.See Tersanctus.
trencher: 1. One who trenches; esp., one who cuts or digs ditches. 2. A large wooden plate or platter, as for table use. 3. The table; hence, the pleasures of the table; food. It could be no ordinary declension of nature that could bring some men, after an ingenuous education, to place their "summum bonum" upon their trenchers. South.
transverse: Lying or being across, or in a crosswise direction; athwart; -- often opposed to Ant: longitudinal. Transverse axis (of an ellipse or hyperbola) (Geom.), that axis which passes through the foci. | 1. Anything that is transverse or athwart. 2. (Geom.) The longer, or transverse, axis of an ellipse.
treason: 1. The offense of attempting to overthrow the government of the state to which the offender owes allegiance, or of betraying the state into the hands of a foreign power; disloyalty; treachery. The treason of the murthering in the bed. Chaucer. Note: In monarchies, the killing of the sovereign, or an attempt to take his life, is treason.
truncated: 1. Cut off; cut short; maimed. 2. (Min.) Replaced, or cut off, by a plane, especially when equally inclined to the adjoining faces; as, a truncated edge. 3. (Zoöl.) Lacking the apex; -- said of certain spiral shells in which the apex naturally drops off.
truculent: 1. Fierce; savage; ferocious; barbarous; as, the truculent inhabitants of Scythia. Ray. 2. Cruel; destructive; ruthless. More or less truculent plagues. Harvey.
tritheism: The opinion or doctrine that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three distinct Gods.
trass: A white to gray volcanic tufa, formed of decomposed trachytic cinders; -- sometimes used as a cement. Hence, a coarse sort of plaster or mortar, durable in water, and used to line cisterns and other reservoirs of water. [Formerly written also tarras, tarrace, terras.] Note: The Dutch trass is made by burning and grinding a soft grayish rock found on the lower Rhine.
transgress: 1. To pass over or beyond; to surpass. Surpassing common faith, transgressing nature's law. Dryden. 2. Hence, to overpass, as any prescribed as the For man will hearken to his glozing lies, And… | To offend against the law; to sin. Who transgressed in the thing accursed. I Chron. ii. 7.
triangulares: The triangular, or maioid, crabs. See Illust. under Maioid, and Illust. of Spider crab, under Spider.
trustworthy: Worthy of trust or confidence; trusty. -- Trust"wor`thi*ness, n.
triliterality: The quality of being triliteral; as, the triliterality of Hebrew roots. W. D. Whitney.
tricorporate: Represented with three bodies conjoined to one head, as a lion.
triglyphical: 1. Consisting of, or pertaining to, triglyphs. 2. Containing three sets of characters or sculptures.
triplex: Havingthree principal operative parts or motions, so as to produce a three-fold effect.
tridacna: A genus of very large marine bivalve shells found on the coral reefs of the Indian and Pacific Oceans. One species (T. gigas) often weighs four or five hundred pounds, and is sometimes used for baptismal fonts. Called also paw shell, and fountain shell.
tripoli: An earthy substance originally brought from Tripoli, used in polishing stones and metals. It consists almost wholly of the siliceous shells of diatoms.
troching: One of the small branches of a stag's antler.
treachery: Violation of allegiance or of faith and confidence; treasonable or perfidious conduct; perfidy; treason. Be ware, ye lords, of their treachery. Chaucer. In the council chamber at Edinburgh, he had contracted a deep taint of treachery and corruption. Macaulay.
trinomial: A quantity consisting of three terms, connected by the sign + or -; as, x + y + z, or ax + 2b - c2. | Consisting of three terms; of or pertaining to trinomials; as, a trinomial root.
trihedral: Having three sides or faces; thus, a trihedral angle is a solid angle bounded by three plane angles. [Written also triedral.]
triform: Having a triple form or character. "This triform antagonism." I. Taylor. Goddess Triform, I own thy triple spell. Lowell.
tridecatylene: A hydrocarbon, C13H26, of the ethylene series, corresponding to tridecane, and obtained from Burmah petroleum as a light colorless liquid; -- called also tridecylene, and tridecene.
trays: Traces. (old) Four white bulls in the trays. Chaucer.
truckler: One who truckles, or yields servilely to the will of another.
trapezoid: 1. (Geom.) A plane four-sided figure, having two sides parallel to each other. 2. (Anat.) A bone of the carpus at the base of the second metacarpal, or index finger. | 1. Having the form of a trapezoid; trapezoidal; as, the trapezoid ligament which connects the coracoid process and the clavicle. 2. (Anat.) Of or pertaining to the trapezoid ligament;
trogue: A wooden trough, forming a drain. Raymond.
triviality: 1. The quality or state of being trivial; trivialness. 2. That which is trivial; a trifle. The philosophy of our times does not expend itself in furious discussions on mere scholastic trivialities. Lyon Playfair.
trumpetweed: (a) An herbaceous composite plant (Eupatorium purpureum), often having hollow stems, and bearing purplish flowers in small corymbed heads. (b) The sea trumpet.
trippingly: In a tripping manner; with a light, nimble, quick step; with agility; nimbly. Sing, and dance it trippingly. Shak. Speak the speech . . . trippingly on the tongue. Shak.
transpass: To pass over; as, Alexander transpassed the river. (old) J. Gregory. | To pass by; to pass away. (old)
trichromic: If, pertaining to, or consisting of, three colors or color sensations. | Containing three atoms of chromium.
triad: 1. A union of three; three objects treated as one; a ternary; a trinity; as, a triad of deities. 2. (Mus.) (a) A chord of three notes. (b) The common chord, consisting of a tone with its third and fifth, with or without the octave. 3. (Chem.) An element or radical whose valence is three.
trim: 1. To make trim; to put in due order for any purpose; to make right, neat, or pleasing; to adjust. The hermit trimmed his little fire. Goldsmith. 2. To dress; to decorate; to adorn; to invest; | To balance; to fluctuate between parties, so as to appear to favor each.
trinitrocellulose: Gun cotton; -- so called because regarded as containing three nitro groups.
tricksy: Exhibiting artfulness; trickish. "My tricksy spirit!" Shak. he tricksy policy which in the seventeenth century passed for state wisdom. Coleridge.
trepidation: 1. An involuntary trembling, sometimes an effect of paralysis, but usually caused by terror or fear; quaking; quivering. 2. Hence, a state of terror or alarm; fear; confusion; fright; as, the men were in great trepidation. 3. (Anc. Astron.) A libration of the starry sphere in the Ptolemaic system;
trammelwheel: A circular plate or a cross, with two or more cross grooves intersecting at the center, used on the end of a shaft to transmit motion to another shaft not in line with the first.
translavation: A laving or lading from one vessel to another. (old) Holland.
transanimate: To animate with a soul conveyed from another body. Bp. J. King (1608).
trichinosis: The disease produced by the presence of trichinæ in the muscles and intestinal track. It is marked by fever, muscular pains, and symptoms resembling those of typhoid fever, and is frequently fatal.
triformity: The state of being triform, or of having a threefold shape.
tribolet: 1. A goldsmith's tool used in making rings. Ainsworth. 2. A steel cylinder round which metal is drawn in the process of forming tubes. Tomlinson. 3. (Blacksmithing) A tapering mandrel.
truce: 1. (Mil.) A suspension of arms by agreement of the commanders of opposing forces; a temporary cessation of hostilities, for negotiation or other purpose; an armistice. 2. Hence, intermission of action, pain, or contest; temporary cessation; short quiet. Where he may likeliest find Truce to his restless thoughts. Milton.
trouble: 1. To put into confused motion; to disturb; to agitate. An angel went down at a certain season into the pool, and troubled the water. John v. 4. God looking forth will trouble all his host. Milton. | Troubled; dark; gloomy. (old) "With full trouble cheer." Chaucer.
trigonocerous: Having horns with three angles, like those of some species of goats.
trabeculate: Crossbarred, as the ducts in a banana stem.
trews: Trowsers; especially, those of the Scotch Highlanders. "He wore the trews, or close trowsers, made of tartan." Sir W. Scott.
triethylamine: A tertiary amine analogous to trimethylamine.
tripitaka: The three divisions, or "baskets" (pitakas), of buddhist scriptures, -- the Vinayapitaka [Skr. Vinayapitsaka] , or Basket of Discipline; Suttapitaka [Pali] , or Basket of Discourses; and Abhidhammapitaka [Pali] , or Basket of Metaphysics.
trapezohedral: Of, pertaining to, or resembling, a trapezohedron.
trisection: The division of a thing into three parts, Specifically: (Geom.) the division of an angle into three equal parts.
truchman: An interpreter. See Dragoman. (old) And after, by the tongue, Her truchman, she reports the mind's each throw. B. Jonson.
tradeswoman: A woman who trades, or is skilled in trade.
transparent: 1. Having the property of transmitting rays of light, so that bodies can be distinctly seen through; pervious to light; diaphanous; pellucid; as, transparent glass; a transparent diamond; -- opposed to Ant: opaque. "Transparent elemental air." Milton. 2. Admitting the passage of light; open; porous; as, a transparent veil. Dryden. Syn. -- Translucent; pellucid; clear; bright;
transubstantiator: One who maintains the doctrine of transubstantiation. Barrow.
transcription: 1. The act or process of transcribing, or copying; as, corruptions creep into books by repeated transcriptions. 2. A copy; a transcript. Walton. 3. (Mus.) An arrangement of a composition for some other instrument or voice than that for which it was originally written, as the translating of a song, a vocal or instrumental quartet, or even an orchestral work, into a piece for…
tritovum: An embryonic insect which has twice cast its skin previous to hatching from the egg.
transflux: A flowing through, across, or beyond.
transfigure: 1. To change the outward form or appearance of; to metamorphose; to transform. 2. Especially, to change to something exalted and glorious; to give an ideal form to. [Jesus] was transfigured before them; and his face did shine as the sun, and his raiment was white as the light. Matt. xvii. 2.
truthteller: One who tells the truth. Truth-teller was our England's Alfred named. Tennyson.
transfugitive: One who flees from one side to another; hence, a deserter; a turncoat; an apostate.
truism: An undoubted or self-evident truth; a statement which is pliantly true; a proposition needing no proof or argument; -- opposed to falsism. Trifling truisms clothed in great, swelling words. J. P. Smith.
trifistulary: Having three pipes. Sir T. Browne.
trachoma: Granular conjunctivitis due to a specific micrococcus. -- Tra*chom"a*tous (#), a.
tryout: A test by which the fitness of a player or contestant to remain in a certain class is determined.
transanimation: The conveyance of a soul from one body to another. Fuller.
tribe: 1. A family, race, or series of generations, descending from the same progenitor, and kept distinct, as in the case of the twelve tribes of Israel, descended from the twelve sons of Jacob. | To distribute into tribes or classes. Our fowl, fish, and quadruped are well tribed. Abp. Nicolson.
troth: 1. Belief; faith; fidelity. Bid her alight And hertroth plight. Shak. 2. Truth; verity; veracity; as, by my troth. Shak. In troth, thou art able to instruct gray hairs. Addison. 3. Betrothal.
transhuman: More than human; superhuman. Words may not tell of that transhuman change. H. F. Cary.
trilemma: 1. (Logic) A syllogism with three conditional propositions, the major premises of which are disjunctively affirmed in the minor. See Dilemma. 2. A state of things in which it is difficult to determine which one of three courses to pursue.
troubadour: One of a school of poets who flourished from the eleventh to the thirteenth century, principally in Provence, in the south of France, and also in the north of Italy. They invented, and especially cultivated, a kind of lyrical poetry characterized by intricacy of meter and rhyme, and usually of a romantic, amatory strain.
trader: 1. One engaged in trade or commerce; one who makes a business of buying and selling or of barter; a merchant; a trafficker; as, a trader to the East Indies; a country trader. 2. A vessel engaged in the coasting or foreign trade.
trimestrial: Of or pertaining to a trimester, or period of three months; occurring once in every three months; quarterly.
trident: 1. (Class Myth.) A kind of scepter or spear with three prongs, -- the common attribute of Neptune. 2. (Rom. Antiq.) A three-pronged spear or goad, used for urging horses; | Having three teeth or prongs; tridentate.
tricoccous: Having three cocci, or roundish carpels. Gray.
trebleness: The quality or state of being treble; as, the trebleness of tones. Bacon.
translunary: Being or lying beyond the moon; hence, ethereal; -- opposed to sublunary. (old) Marlowe, bathed in the Thespian springs, Had in him those brave, translunary things That the first poets had. Drayton.
transnature: To transfer or transform the nature of. (old) We are transelemented, or transnatured. Jewel.
tractility: The quality of being tractile; ductility. Derham.
trave: 1. (Arch.) A crossbeam; a lay of joists. Maundrell. 2. A wooden frame to confine an unruly horse or ox while shoeing. She sprung as a colt doth in the trave. Chaucer.
trickster: One who tricks; a deceiver; a tricker; a cheat.
trinoctial: Lasting during three nights; comprising three nights.
travers: Across; athwart. (old) The earl . . . caused . . . high trees to be hewn down, and laid travers one over another. Ld. Berners.
trammeler: 1. One who uses a trammel net. Nares. 2. One who, or that which, trammels or restrains.
trawler: 1. One who, or that which, trawls. 2. A fishing vessel which trails a net behind it.
trisnitrate: A nitrate formed from three molecules of nitric acid; also, less properly, applied to certain basic nitrates; as, trisnitrate of bismuth.
trichinoscope: An apparatus for the detection of trichinæ in the flesh of animals, as of swine.
trematodea: An extensive order of parasitic worms. They are found in the internal cavities of animals belonging to all classes. Many species are found, also, on the gills and skin of fishes. transformation: The act of transforming, or the state of being transformed; change of form or condition. Specifically: --(a) (Biol.) troutbird: The American golden plover. [Local, U. S.]
traumatic: (a) Of or pertaining to wounds; applied to wounds. Coxe. (b) Adapted to the cure of wounds; vulnerary. Wiseman. (c) Produced by wounds; as, traumatic tetanus. -- n. A traumatic medicine.
trommel: A revolving buddle or sieve for separating, or sizing, ores. Raymond.
trimesitic: Of, pertaining to, or designating, a tribasic acid, C6H3.(CO2)3, of the aromatic series, obtained, by the oxidation of mesitylene, as a white crystalline substance. [Written also trimesic.]
trickish: Given to tricks; artful in making bargains; given to deception and cheating; knavish. -- Trick"ish*ly, adv. -- Trick"ish*ness, n.
trichite: 1. (Min.) A kind of crystallite resembling a bunch of hairs, common in obsidian. See Illust. of Crystallite. 2. (Zoöl.) A delicate, hairlike siliceous spicule, found in certain sponges. tracheocele: (a) Goiter. (b) A tumor containing air and communicating with the trachea. Morell Mackenzie.
transcolation: Act of transcolating, or state of being transcolated. (old) Bp. Stillingfleet.
trademark: A peculiar distinguishing mark or device affixed by a manufacturer or a merchant to his goods, the exclusive right of using which is recognized by law.
triseriate: Arranged in three vertical or spiral rows.
troche: A medicinal tablet or lozenge; strictly, one of circular form.
trysail: A fore-and-aft sail, bent to a gaff, and hoisted on a lower mast or on a small mast, called the trysail mast, close abaft a lower mast; -- used chiefly as a storm sail. Called also spencer. Totten.
trusion: The act of pushing or thrusting. Bentley.
triungulus: The active young larva of any oil beetle. It has feet armed with three claws, and is parasitic on bees. See Illust. of Oil beetle, under Oil.
tributer: One who works for a certain portion of the ore, or its value. Weale.
transfeminate: To change into a woman, as a man. [Obs. & R.] Sir T. Browne.
triadelphous: Having stamens joined by filaments into three bundles. See Illust. under Adelphous.
triable: 1. Fit or possible to be tried; liable to be subjected to trial or test. "Experiments triable." Boyle. 2. (Law) Liable to undergo a judicial examination; properly coming under the cognizance of a court; as, a cause may be triable before one court which is not triable in another.
trinket: A three-cornered sail formerly carried on a ship's foremast, probably on a lateen yard. Sailing always with the sheets of mainsail and trinket warily in our hands. Hakluyt. | 1. A knife; a cutting tool. Tusser. 2. A small ornament, as a jewel, ring, or the like. 3. A thing of little value; a trifle; a toy.
truebred: 1. Of a genuine or right breed; as, a true-bred beast. Shak. 2. Being of real breeding or education; as, a true-bred gentleman.
trochlear: Shaped like, or resembling, a pulley; pertaining to, or connected with, a trochlea; as, a trochlear articular surface; the trochlear muscle of the eye. Trochlear nerve. See Pathetic nerve, under Pathetic.
tribromphenol: A colorless crystalline substance prepared by the reaction of carbolic acid with bromine.
transience: The quality of being transient; transientness.
transfusive: Tending to transfuse; having power to transfuse.
trisected: Divided into three parts or segments by incisions extending to the midrib or to the base; -- said of leaves.
tradeless: Having no trade or traffic. Young.
trusteeprocess: The process of attachment by garnishment. [U. S.]
triadic: Having the characteristics of a triad; as, boron is triadic.
trochometer: A contrivance for computing the revolutions of a wheel; an odometer.
trading: 1. Carrying on trade or commerce; engaged in trade; as, a trading company. 2. Frequented by traders. "They on the trading flood." Milton. 3. Venal; corrupt; jobbing; as, a trading politician.
triticin: A carbohydrate isomeric with dextrin, obtained from quitch grass (Agropyrum, formerly Triticum, repens) as a white amorphous substance.
trichinize: To render trichinous; to affect with trichinæ; -- chiefly used in the past participle; as, trichinized pork.
treatable: Manageable; tractable; hence, moderate; not violent. (old) " A treatable disposition, a strong memory." R. Parr. A kind of treatable dissolution. Hooker. The heats or the colds of seasons are less treatable than with us. Sir W. Temple.
trachelobranchiate: Having the gills situated upon the neck; -- said of certain mollusks.
transpiration: 1. (Physiol.) trisyllabic: Of or pertaining to a trisyllable; consisting of three syllables; as, "syllable" is a trisyllabic word. -- Tris`yllab"ic*al*ly, adv.
trekker: One that treks. [Written also trecker.] [South Africa] James Bryce.
truthless: Devoid of truth; dishonest; dishonest; spurious; faithless. -- Truth"less*ness, n.
truncate: Appearing as if cut off at the tip; as, a truncate leaf or feather.
trace: One of two straps, chains, or ropes of a harness, extending from the collar or breastplate to a whiffletree attached to a vehicle or thing to be drawn; a tug. | 1. tramp: 1. To tread upon forcibly and repeatedly; to trample. 2. To travel or wander through; as, to tramp the country. [Colloq.] 3. To cleanse, as clothes, by treading upon them in water. [Scot.] Jamieson. | To travel; to wander; to stroll.
transfixion: The act of transfixing, or the state of being transfixed, or pierced. Bp. Hall.
trawlwarp: A rope passing through a block, used in managing or dragging a trawlnet.
troopmeal: By troops; in crowds. (old) So, troopmeal, Troy pursued a while, laying on with swords and darts. Chapman.
trundletail: A round or curled-up tail; also, a dog with such a tail. Shak.
trisyllabical: Of or pertaining to a trisyllable; consisting of three syllables; as, "syllable" is a trisyllabic word. -- Tris`yllab"ic*al*ly, adv.
trafficable: Capable of being disposed of in traffic; marketable. (old) Bp. Hall.
triamide: An amide containing three amido groups.
tryst: 1. Trust. (old) 2. An appointment to meet; also, an appointed place or time of meeting; as, to keep tryst; to break tryst. trigesimosecundo: Having thirty-two leaves to a sheet; as, a trigesimo-secundo form, book, leaf, size, etc. | A book composed of sheets so folded that each one makes thirty- two leaves; hence, indicating, more or less definitely, a size of book; -- usually written 32mo, or 32º, and called thirty-twomo.
troy: Troy weight. Troy weight, the weight which gold and silver, jewels, and the like, are weighed. It was so named from Troyes, in France, where it was first adopted in Europe. transexion: Change of sex. (old) Sir T. Browne.
tripery: A place where tripe is prepared or sold. London Quart. Rev.
transplendency: Quality or state of being transplendent. Dr. H. More.
transgression: The act of transgressing, or of passing over or beyond any law, civil or moral; the violation of a law or known principle of rectitude; breach of command; fault; offense; crime; sin. trustless: That may not be trusted; not worthy of trust; unfaithful. -- Trust"less*ness, n.

trow: A boat with an open well amidships. It is used in spearing fish. Knight. | To believe; to trust; to think or suppose. (old) So that ye trow in Christ, and you baptize. Chaucer. A better priest, I trow, there nowhere none is. Chaucer. It never yet was worn, I trow. Tennyson.
tracheobronchial: Pertaining both to the tracheal and bronchial tubes, or to their junction; -- said of the syrinx of certain birds.
trubu: An East India herring (Clupea toli) which is extensively caught for the sake of its roe and for its flesh.
transliteration: The act or product of transliterating, or of expressing words of a language by means of the characters of another alphabet.
traditionalist: An advocate of, or believer in, traditionalism; a traditionist.
trochlea: 1. (Mach.) A pulley. (old) 2. (Anat.) A pulley, or a structure resembling a pulley; as, the trochlea, or pulleylike end, of the humerus, which articulates with the ulna; or the trochlea, or fibrous ring, in the upper part of the orbit, through which the superior oblique, or trochlear, muscle of the eye passes.
traiteur: The keeper of an eating house, or restaurant; a restaurateur. Simmonds.
triskelion: A figure composed of three branches, usually curved, radiating from a center, as the figure composed of three human legs, with bent knees, which has long been used as a badge or symbol of Sicily and of the Isle of Man.
treeful: The quantity or number which fills a tree.
treckschuyt: A covered boat for goods and passengers, used on the Dutch and Flemish canals.
transvection: The act of conveying or carrying over.
truthy: Truthful; likely; probable. "A more truthy import." W. G. Palgrave.
tropaeolin: A name given to any one of a series of orange-red dyestuffs produced artificially from certain complex sulphonic acid derivatives of azo and diazo hydrocarbons of the aromatic series; -- so called because of the general resemblance to the shades of nasturtium (Tropæolum).
traducement: The act of traducing; misrepresentation; ill-founded censure; defamation; calumny. Shak.
trone: A small drain. [Obs. or Prov. Eng.] | 1. A steelyard. [Prov. Eng.] 2. A form of weighing machine for heavy wares, consisting of two horizontal bars crossing each other, beaked at the extremities, and supported by a wooden pillar.
tripestone: A variety of anhydrite composed of contorted plates fancied to resemble pieces of tripe.
tracker: 1. One who, or that which, tracks or pursues, as a man or dog that follows game. And of the trackers of the deer Scarce half the lessening pack was near. Sir W. Scott. 2. (Mus.) In the organ, a light strip of wood connecting (in path) a key and a pallet, to communicate motion by pulling.
trinity: 1. (Christian Theol.) The union of three persons (the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost) in one Godhead, so that all the three are one God as to substance, but three persons as to individuality. 2. Any union of three in one; three units treated as one; a triad, as the Hindoo trinity, or Trimurti. 3.
truismatic: Of or pertaining to truisms; consisting of truisms.
transilience: A leap across or from one thing to another. "An unadvised transiliency." Glanvill.
tridiapason: A triple octave, or twenty-second. Busby.
translucency: The quality or state of being translucent; clearness; partial transparency. Sir T. Browne.
tretis: A treatise; also, a treaty. (old) Chaucer. | Long and well-proportioned; nicely made; pretty. (old) "Her nose tretys." Chaucer.
trimurti: The triad, or trinity, of Hindoo gods, consisting of Brahma, the Creator, Vishnu, the Preserver, and Siva, the Destroyer. [Spelled also Trimurtti.]
trapeziform: Having the form of a trapezium; trapezoid.
triflorous: Three-flowered; having or bearing three flowers; as, a triflorous peduncle.
transmutationist: One who believes in the transmutation of metals or of species.
trammel: 1. A kind of net for catching birds, fishes, or other prey. Carew. 2. A net for confining a woman's hair. Spenser. 3. A kind of shackle used for regulating the motions of a horse and making him… | 1. To entangle, as in a net; to catch. Shak. 2. To confine; to hamper; to shackle.
triassic: Of the age of, or pertaining to, the Trias. -- n. The Triassic formation.
transisthmian: Extending across an isthmus, as at Suez or Panama.
transmeation: The act of transmeating; a passing through or beyond. (old)
tragedienne: A woman who plays in tragedy.
trigonid: The cutting region of the crown of an upper molar, usually the anterior part. That of a lower molar is the Tri"go*nid.
triennial: 1. Continuing three years; as, triennial parliaments; a triennial reign. Howell. 2. Happening, coming about, or appearing once in every three years; as, triennial elections; a triennial catalogue; | Something which takes place or appears once in three years.
trisulc: Something having three forks or prongs, as a trident. (old) "Jupiter's trisulc." Sir T. Browne.
trimethylamine: A colorless volatile alkaline liquid, N.(CH3)3, obtained from herring brine, beet roots, etc., with a characteristic herringlike odor. It is regarded as a substituted ammonia containing three methyl groups.
trepanize: To trepan. (old) "By trepanizing the skull." Jer. Taylor.
trumpeter: 1. One who sounds a trumpet. 2. One who proclaims, publishes, or denounces. These men are good trumpeters. Bacon. 3. (Zoöl.) (a) Any one of several species of long-legged South American birds of the genus Psophia, especially P. crepitans, which is abundant, and often domesticated and kept with other poultry by the natives. They are allied to the cranes.
trapan: A snare; a stratagem; a trepan. See 3d Trepan. South. | To insnare; to catch by stratagem; to entrap; to trepan. Having some of his people trapanned at Baldivia. Anson.
trot: 1. To proceed by a certain gait peculiar to quadrupeds; to ride or drive at a trot. See Trot, n. 2. Fig.: To run; to jog; to hurry. He that rises late must trot all day, and will scarcely overtake… | To cause to move, as a horse or other animal, in the pace called a trot; to cause to run without galloping or cantering. tralatitious: 1. Passed along; handed down; transmitted. Among biblical critics a tralatitious interpretation is one received by expositor from expositor. W. Withington. 2. Metaphorical; figurative; not literal. Stackhouse.
tricurvate: Curved in three directions; as, a tricurvate spicule (see Illust. of Spicule).
trape: To walk or run about in an idle or slatternly manner; to traipse. [Obs. or Colloq.]
tropine: A white crystalline alkaloid, C8H15NO, produced by decomposing atropine.
trainoil: Oil procured from the blubber or fat of whales, by boiling.
tritical: Trite. (old) T. Warton. -- Trit"ic*al*ly, adv. (old) -- Trit"ic*al*ness, n. (old)
trochanteric: Of or pertaining to one or both of the trochanters.
trional: A compound similar to sulphonal, used as a hypnotic in medicine.
trirectangular: Having three right angles. See Triquadrantal.
transcursion: A rambling or ramble; a passage over bounds; an excursion. (old) Howell.
tridactyle: Having three fingers or toes, or composed of three movable parts attached to a common base.
trifurcated: Having three branches or forks; trichotomous.
transfluent: 1. Flowing or running across or through; as, a transfluent stream. 2. (Her.) Passing or flowing through a bridge; -- said of water. Wright.
trope: (a) The use of a word or expression in a different sense from that which properly belongs to it; the use of a word or expression as changed from the original signification to another, for the sake of giving life or emphasis to an idea; a figure of speech. (b) The word or expression so used.
troglodytical: Of or pertaining to a troglodyte, or dweller in caves.
transitoriness: The quality or state of being transitory; speedy passage or departure.
trackway: Any of two or more narrow paths, of steel, smooth stone, or the like, laid in a public roadway otherwise formed of an inferior pavement, as cobblestones, to provide an easy way for wheels.
transitory: Continuing only for a short time; not enduring; fleeting; evanescent. Comfort and succor all those who, in this transitory life, are in trouble. Bk. of Com. Prayer. It was not the transitory light of a comet, which shines and glows for a wile, and then . . . vanishes into nothing. South.
triumphing: Having or celebrating a triumph; victorious; triumphant. -- Tri"umph*ing*ly, adv.
trample: 1. To tread under foot; to tread down; to prostrate by treading; as, to trample grass or flowers. Dryden. Neither cast ye your pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet. Matt. vii. | 1. To tread with force and rapidity; to stamp. 2. To tread in contempt; -- with on or upon. Diogenes trampled on Plato's pride with greater of his own. Gov. of Tongue.
trait: 1. A stroke; a touch. By this single trait Homer makes an essential difference between the Iliad and Odyssey. Broome. 2. A distinguishing or marked feature; a peculiarity; as, a trait of character. Note: Formerly pronounced tra, as in French, and still so pronounced to some extent in England.
tritheistical: Of or pertaining to tritheism. Bolingbroke.
tripudiary: Of or pertaining to dancing; performed by dancing. " Tripudiary augurations." Sir T. Browne.
transported: Conveyed from one place to another; figuratively, carried away with passion or pleasure; entranced. -- Trans*port"ed*ly, adv. -- Trans*port"ed*ness, n.
tripalmitate: A palmitate derived from three molecules of palmitic acid.
troilusbutterfly: A large American butterfly (Papilio troilus). It is black, with yellow marginal spots on the front wings, and blue on the rear.
transmigratory: Passing from one body or state to another.
try: 1. To divide or separate, as one sort from another; to winnow; to sift; to pick out; -- frequently followed by out; as, to try out the wild corn from the good. (old) Sir T. Elyot. 2. | 1. tridactyl: Having three fingers or toes, or composed of three movable parts attached to a common base.
triarian: Occupying the third post or rank. (old) Cowley.
traffic: 1. To pass goods and commodities from one person to another for an equivalent in goods or money; to buy or sell goods; to barter; to trade. 2. To trade meanly or mercenarily; to bargain. | To exchange in traffic; to effect by a bargain or for a consideration.
transmissive: Capable of being transmitted; derived, or handed down, from one to another. Itself a sun, it with transmissive light Enlivens worlds denied to human sight. Prior.
traduction: 1. Transmission from one to another. (old) Traditional communication and traduction of truths. Sir M. Hale. 2. Translation from one language to another. (old) 3. The act of transferring; conveyance; transportation.
transpositional: Of or pertaining to transposition; involving transposition. Pegge.

tranquil: Quiet; calm; undisturbed; peaceful; not agitated; as, the atmosphere is tranquil; the condition of the country is tranquil. A style clear, tranquil, easy to follow. De Quincey.
transumpt: A copy or exemplification of a record. (old) Lord Herbert.
tranquilness: Quality or state of being tranquil.
triglyphic: 1. Consisting of, or pertaining to, triglyphs. 2. Containing three sets of characters or sculptures.
treadwheel: A wheel turned by persons or animals, by treading, climbing, or pushing with the feet, upon its periphery or face. See Treadmill.
treat: 1. To handle; to manage; to use; to bear one's self toward; as, to treat prisoners cruelly; to treat children kindly. 2. trajectory: The curve which a body describes in space, as a planet or comet in its orbit, or stone thrown upward obliquely in the air.
tressure: A kind of border similar to the orle, but of only half the breadth of the latter.

trichloride: A chloride having three atoms of chlorine in the molecule.
trimorphous: Of, pertaining to, or characterized by, trimorphism; -- contrasted with monomorphic, dimorphic, and polymorphic.
tretys: A treatise; also, a treaty. (old) Chaucer. | Long and well-proportioned; nicely made; pretty. (old) "Her nose tretys." Chaucer.
trenchplough: To plow with deep furrows, for the purpose of loosening the land to a greater depth than usual.
trapezoidal: 1. Having the form of a trapezoid; trapezoid. 2. (Min.) Tranpezohedral.
trigynian: Having three pistils or styles; of or pertaining to the Trigynia.

transportability: The quality or state of being transportable.
transcur: To run or rove to and fro. (old) Bacon.

trousering: Cloth or material for making trousers.
traitorous: 1. Guilty of treason; treacherous; perfidious; faithless; as, a traitorous officer or subject. Shak. 2. Consisting in treason; partaking of treason; implying breach of allegiance; as, a traitorous scheme. -- Trai"tor*ous*ly, adv. -- Trai"tor*ous*ness, n.
treeburial: Disposal of the dead by placing the corpse among the branches of a tree or in a hollow trunk, a practice among many primitive peoples.
tralucency: Translucency; as, the tralucency of a gem. (old) Sir T. Browne.
tragedy: 1. A dramatic poem, composed in elevated style, representing a signal action performed by some person or persons, and having a fatal issue; that species of drama which represents the sad or terrible phases of character and life.
tringle: A curtain rod for a bedstead.
tracheophonae: A group of passerine birds having the syrinx at the lower end of the trachea.

trichiasis: A disease of the eye, in which the eyelashes, being turned in upon the eyeball, produce constant irritation by the motion of the lids.
trisplanchnic: Of or pertaining to the three great splanchnic cavities, namely, that of the head, the chest, and the abdomen; -- applied to the sympathetic nervous system.

transcendentality: The quality or state of being transcendental.
triumphant: 1. Rejoicing for victory; triumphing; exultant. Successful beyond hope to lead ye forth Triumphant out of this infernal pit. Milton. 2. Celebrating victory; expressive of joy for success; as, a triumphant song or ode. 3. Graced with conquest; victorious. Athena, war's triumphant maid. Pope. So shall it be in the church triumphant. Perkins. 4. Of or pertaining to triumph;
tractile: Capable of being drawn out in length; ductile. Bacon.
tradition: 1. The act of delivering into the hands of another; delivery. "A deed takes effect only from the tradition or delivery." Blackstone. 2. The unwritten or oral delivery of information, opinions,… | To transmit by way of tradition; to hand down. (old) The following story is . . . traditioned with very much credit amongst our English Catholics. Fuller.
trachelipoda: An extensive artificial group of gastropods comprising all those which have a spiral shell and the foot attached to the base of the neck.
tranter: One who trants; a peddler; a carrier. [Written also traunter.] [Obs. or Prov. Eng.]
tradesunionist: A member of a trades union, or a supporter of trades unions.
truculence: The quality or state of being truculent; savageness of manners; ferociousness.
trabea: A toga of purple, or ornamented with purple horizontal stripes. -- worn by kings, consuls, and augurs. Dr. W. Smith.
trickle: To flow in a small, gentle stream; to run in drops. His salt tears trickled down as rain. Chaucer. Fast beside there trickled softly down A gentle stream. Spenser.
transplant: 1. To remove, and plant in another place; as, to transplant trees. Dryden. 2. To remove, and settle or establish for residence in another place; as, to transplant inhabitants. Being transplanted out of his cold, barren diocese of St. David into a warmer climate. Clarendon.
trollmydames: The game of nineholes. [Written also trolmydames.] (old) Shak.
trophonian: Of or pertaining to Trophonius, his architecture, or his cave and oracle.
transpose: 1. To change the place or order of; to substitute one for the other of; to exchange, in respect of position; as, to transpose letters, words, or propositions. 2. To change; to transform; to invert. Things base and vile, holding no quantity, Love can transpose to form and dignity. Shak. 3.
tradeunion: An organized combination among workmen for the purpose of maintaining their rights, privileges, and interests with respect to wages, hours of labor, customs, etc.
trumpery: 1. Deceit; fraud. (old) Grenewey. 2. Something serving to deceive by false show or pretense; falsehood; deceit; worthless but showy matter; hence, things worn out and of no value; rubbish. | Worthless or deceptive in character. "A trumpery little ring." Thackeray.
trainband: A band or company of an organized military force instituted by James I. and dissolved by Charles II.; -- afterwards applied to the London militia. [Eng.] He felt that, without some better protection than that of the trainbands and Beefeaters, his palace and person would hardly be secure. Macaulay. A trainband captain eke was he Of famous London town. Cowper.
trueness: The quality of being true; reality; genuineness; faithfulness; sincerity; exactness; truth.
traducible: 1. Capable of being derived or propagated. (old) Sir M. Hale. 2. Capable of being traduced or calumniated.
trireme: An ancient galley or vessel with tree banks, or tiers, of oars.
transgressor: One who transgresses; one who breaks a law, or violates a command; one who violates any known rule or principle of rectitude; a sinner. The way of transgressors is hard. Prov. xiii. 15.
transvasate: To pour out of one vessel into another. (old) Cudworth.
travertine: A white concretionary form of calcium carbonate, usually hard and semicrystalline. It is deposited from the water of springs or streams holding lime in solution. Extensive deposits exist at Tivoli, near Rome.
trigraph: Three letters united in pronunciation so as to have but one sound, or to form but one syllable, as -ieu in adieu; a triphthong.
tribometer: An instrument to ascertain the degree of friction in rubbing surfaces. Brande & C.
treasurystock: Issued stock of an incorporated company held by the company itself.
transplanter: One who transplants; also, a machine for transplanting trees.
truite: Having a delicately crackled surface; --applied to porcelian, etc.
transfuge: One who flees from one side to another; hence, a deserter; a turncoat; an apostate.
transposition: The act of transposing, or the state of being transposed. Specifically: --(a) (Alg.) The bringing of any term of an equation from one side over to the other without destroying the equation. (b) (Gram.) A change of the natural order of words in a sentence; as, the Latin and Greek languages admit transposition, without inconvenience, to a much greater extent than the English.
transudation: 1. The act or process of transuding. 2. (Physics) Same as Exosmose.
transcalency: The quality or state of being transcalent.
triternate: Three times ternate; -- applied to a leaf whose petiole separates into three branches, each of which divides into three parts which each bear three leafiets.
trolleycar: A motor car to which the current is conveyed by means of a trolley.
tragicomical: Of or pertaining to tragi-comedy; partaking of grave and comic scenes. -- Trag`-com"ic*al*ly, adv. Julian felt toward him that tragi-comic sensation which makes us pity the object which excites it not the less that we are somewhat inclined to laugh amid our sympathy. Sir W. Scott.
trones: 1. A steelyard. [Prov. Eng.] 2. A form of weighing machine for heavy wares, consisting of two horizontal bars crossing each other, beaked at the extremities, and supported by a wooden pillar. It is now mostly disused. [Scot.] Jamieson. Trone stone, a weight equivalent to nineteen and a half pounds.
transpassable: Capable of being transpassed, or crossed over. (old)
tridentine: Of or pertaining to Trent, or the general church council held in that city.
traceable: Capable of being traced. -- Trace"a*ble*ness, n. -- Trace"a/bly, adv.
triduan: Lasting three lays; also, happening every third day. Blount.
troopship: A vessel built or fitted for the conveyance of troops; a transport. [Eng.]
trikosane: A hydrocarbon, C23H48, of the methane series, resembling paraffin; -- so called because it has twenty-three atoms of carbon in the molecule.
trustee: A person to whom property is legally committed in trust, to be applied either for the benefit of specified individuals, or for public uses; one who is intrusted with property for the benefit of… | 1. To commit (property) to the care of a trustee; as, to trustee an estate. 2. (Law) To attach (a debtor's wages, credits, or property in the hands of a third person) in the interest of the creditor.
trimorphism: 1. (Crystallog.) The property of crystallizing in three forms fundamentally distinct, as is the case with titanium dioxide, which crystallizes in the forms of rutile, octahedrite, and brookite. See Pleomorphism. 2. (Biol.) The coëxistence among individuals of the same species of three distinct forms, not connected, as a rule, by intermediate gradations;
treasury: 1. A place or building in which stores of wealth are deposited; especially, a place where public revenues are deposited and kept, and where money is disbursed to defray the expenses of government; hence, also, the place of deposit and disbursement of any collected funds. 2. That department of a government which has charge of the finances. 3. A repository of abundance;
tracheate: Breathing by means of tracheæ; of or pertaining to the Tracheata. | Any arthropod having tracheæ; one of the Tracheata.
tricorporal: Represented with three bodies conjoined to one head, as a lion.
trifarious: Facing three ways; arranged in three vertical ranks, as the leaves of veratrum.
transcribbler: A transcriber; -- used in contempt. He [Aristotle] has suffered vastly from the transcribblers, as all authors of great brevity necessarily must. Gray.
transpatronize: To transfer the patronage of. (old) Warner.
triple: 1. Consisting of three united; multiplied by three; threefold; as, a triple knot; a triple tie. By thy triple shape as thou art seen. Dryden. 2. Three times repeated; treble. See Treble. 3. | To make threefold, or thrice as much or as many; to treble; as, to triple the tax on coffee.
